title: Hiro, Moku and the Haiku
blurb: The new classroom robot can solve any sum in a blink, but it cannot write a poem. Hiro has a week to teach it.

chapters.title: A Robot in Class Five
chapters.text:
On Monday morning, a silver robot rolled into Class Five at Hiro's school in Kyoto. It had round blue eyes, a square head and a small screen on its chest. "Hello, everyone," it said. "My name is Moku. I can solve any sum, spell any word and count every leaf in the playground."

The children cheered. Their teacher, Ms Tanaka, smiled. "Moku will be our classroom helper," she said. "And this week we have a special project. Each of you will write a haiku for the school festival on Friday."

Hiro groaned quietly. He liked football and science, not poems, and he did not like the idea at all. His friend Mei nudged him. "Moku will help you," she whispered.

"I will certainly try," said the robot. "Please explain the word haiku."

chapters.title: Five, Seven, Five
chapters.text:
Ms Tanaka explained. "A haiku is a very short poem from Japan. It has three lines. The first line has five syllables, the second has seven, and the third has five again. Most haiku are about nature or a season."

"Syllables are the beats in a word," said Hiro. "Like but-ter-fly has three."

Moku's blue eyes flickered. After two seconds it said, "I have written one." It read in a flat voice: "Rain falls from the sky. Three millimetres per day. Rain is wet and cold."

The class tried not to laugh, and nobody spoke for a moment. "The syllables are perfect," Mei said kindly. "But there is something missing."

"What is missing?" asked Moku. "I counted five, seven and five."

Hiro stared at his own empty page. He knew exactly how Moku felt.

chapters.title: Listening in the Garden
chapters.text:
On Tuesday, Hiro had an idea. After school he took Moku to the old temple garden near his house. The leaves of the maple trees were red and orange, and a gentle breeze moved the bamboo.

"A haiku starts with noticing," Hiro said. "Do not count. Just look and listen." He sat on a stone bench and Moku stood beside him.

"I notice twenty-seven maple leaves on the ground," said Moku.

"No numbers," laughed Hiro. "What do you hear?"

Moku turned its head. Then it heard a soft knock, tock, from a bamboo water pipe in the corner. Water filled the pipe, tipped over and knocked on a stone. Moku was silent for a long time.

"It is a very small sound," it said at last. "But it makes the whole garden feel quiet."

chapters.title: A Warm Processor
chapters.text:
That night, Moku sat at Hiro's desk in the corner of the classroom, where Ms Tanaka let it charge. A small light blinked on its chest. Hiro sat next to it, trying to write a line about football and failing.

"Hiro," said Moku. "My processor is warm. It is not overheating, and I have checked. When I think about the garden, something changes inside me. Is this what you call a feeling?"

"I think so," said Hiro. "It sounds like wonder."

"Then I should like to write it down." Moku's eyes blinked slowly. A moment later it read aloud:

"Red leaf falls slowly. The water drips in bamboo. Autumn holds its breath."

Hiro counted on his fingers: five, seven, five. His eyes grew wide. "That is a real haiku, Moku. It is a good one."

chapters.title: Festival Day
chapters.text:
On Friday, the school hall was full of parents, lanterns and paper cranes. Each class stood on the stage and read their haiku. Hiro waited at the side with Moku, his hands shaking.

Daiki from Class Six walked past and snorted. "A robot writing a poem? That is silly. It will only count syllables."

"Perhaps," said Moku calmly. "But I will try something new."

When Class Five's turn came, Mei read first. Then others followed. At last Ms Tanaka said, "Hiro and Moku, please."

Hiro walked to the microphone and took a deep breath. "We wrote two haiku," he said. "One by Moku, and one by me."

His voice shook at first, but then he looked at Moku's blue eyes and felt braver. Behind him, the robot was holding the page very still.

chapters.title: What Moku Learned
chapters.text:
Moku read first, in a soft voice that no one had heard before. The hall fell quiet when it said, "Autumn holds its breath." Someone near the back sighed. Then Hiro read his own haiku:

"Moku's blue eyes glow. Learning how to hear the rain. We are both quiet."

For a moment nobody moved. Then the whole hall began to clap. Even Daiki clapped, though he pretended to scratch his ear at the same time.

Ms Tanaka gave them a special card for the festival: Best Pair. On the way home, Hiro asked, "What did you learn, Moku?"

The robot considered carefully. "I cannot count a feeling," it said. "But I can notice one. And I think I learned that from a friend."

Hiro grinned. "Next week," he said, "I will teach you football."
